Reports, papers, letters, manuals and covers get their own blocks. All of them work in Writeout, Bitbook, Amber and anywhere else Keydown runs, print cleanly, and turn back into plain text when you Un-format. One line each: ::toc 3 numbered Contents builds a table of contents from your headings (the number is the deepest heading level, and numbered adds 1.2.3 numbers). Click an entry to jump. ::cover Title Subtitle Author Date is a cover page that ends with a page break. ::banner Title Subtitle blue is a colored title band. ::wordcount shows words, reading time and characters; ::date (or ::date iso , short , year ) writes today's date. ::footnotes Notes lists every footnote, ::lof lists figures and ::lot lists tables. ::stamp DRAFT red is a tilted rubber stamp, ::watermark CONFIDENTIAL puts a big faint word behind the page. ::sign Name, Title and ::signatures Alice Bob draw signature lines. ::keywords one, two, three makes keyword pills, ::lorem 3 fills in placeholder paragraphs, ::space 4 leaves four lines of room. From ::name to ::end : ::note , ::tip , ::info , ::warning , ::danger , ::success and ::important are colored callout boxes ( ::note Your own title ). ::callout warning Title works too. ::columns 3 splits the text into columns; put on its own line to choose where each column starts. ::tabs with @tab Name lines, and ::accordion with @item Title lines, hide text until

Writeout and Bitbook have two ways to write a table. Pipe tables : one row per line, like Name Score , with a line of --- --- under the header row. Add a style after it, like --- --- {green} . The styles are blue (the default), green , purple , amber , plain and dark , plus four flat ones with no gradients or shadows: flat (gray, with a big rounded outline, thick lines between the cells, a darker header row and stripes) and its tinted cousins flatblue , flatgreen and flatpurple . Cell by cell : @@table [a1h:'Name',b1:'Score',a2:'Ann',b2:' O 9 '] names each cell like a spreadsheet (columns a to o, rows 1 and up) and gives its text in quotes. The text can use any Keydown, like chips and bold , and \' writes a quote. A style can follow the ] , like {green} . In a cell-by-cell table, an h after the cell name makes a header. A row is a header row when its first cell is a header ( a1h ), and then its whole row is headers. An h cell on any other row moves up to the nearest header row above it. Another header row further down starts a new part of the table: @@table [a1h:'Name',b1h:'Score',a2:'Ann',b2:' O 9 ',c3h:'Bonus',a4h:'Round 2',b4:'Score',a5:'Bob',b5:' 7 ']{green}

Writeout and Bitbook save their files (.kd and .kn) as Keydown text: a short header with the page size and other settings, then the document itself, readable in any text editor. When a file opens, the text turns back into formatting. A few extra spellings cover what the toolbar makes: Colors, fonts and sizes : [words]{color dc2626} colors the words, like [these words]{color dc2626}. bg gives a background, like [a marker]{bg fde047}, font "Georgia" picks a font, size 24px a size and weight 600 a weight. They can be combined: [big blue words]{color 2563eb size 20px weight 700} gives [big blue words]{color 2563eb size 20px weight 700}. Alignment : a line starting with {align center} is centered; right and justify work too. Pictures and files : a picture you inserted is saved right in the file as !name , with {width 240px} after it when you resized it. An attached file is report.pdf{file} . Tabs : each tab of a document starts with a line like ::tab{name "Ideas"} . Plain symbols : words that only look like Keydown keep their symbols as themselves, with a backslash, like \ R\ not a highlight\ \ .

Open a fence with a language and a style in curly braces, and add a title after a bar! npm run build The styles are terminal, mac, dark, paper, blueprint, neon, ember, gel and diff. Add the word lines for line numbers, as in js{dark lines app.js}. The diff style tints lines that start with + or -! Inline code takes a style too, like ls -la {terminal}, Cmd {key} or x {neon}. The inline styles are terminal, dark, paper, blueprint, neon, ember, gel and key!

Page breaks A line that is only ::pagebreak is a page break. In Writeout's Pages view the text after it starts on a fresh page, and printing starts a new page there too. Writeout's New Page button (or Ctrl/Cmd+Enter) puts one at the caret, and Backspace at the start of the next line takes it away. Divider styles ::divider draws the aqua strip. Put a style in the braces for another look, like ::divider{wavy} , and add a title after a to run the line on both sides of it, like ::divider{poolside Lap two} . The styles are aqua, poolside, dual, notched, wavy, dotted, dashed, zigzag, glow, ruler, stitched, bubbles, scallop, neon, arrows, fade, swallow, triple, stepped, crest, ticket, gel, glass and rim. ::divider{aqua} the original aqua strip {aqua} ::divider{poolside} plain orange dashed lines, no special effects at all {poolside} ::divider{dual} a thick and a thin rail {dual} ::divider{notched} pointed ends and a V notch in the middle {notched} ::divider{wavy} a rolling wave {wavy} ::divider{dotted} a row of gel beads {dotted} ::divider{dashed} rounded dashes {dashed} ::divider{zigzag} a zigzag {zigzag} ::divider{glow} a neon line that fades out at both ends {glow} ::divider{ruler} ruler tick marks {ruler} ::divider{stitched} orange stitches {stitched} ::divider{bubbles} bubbles rising in the water {bubbles} ::divider{scallop} a row of little arcs ::divider{neon} a thin glowing tub

::blank{style rows Label} leaves an empty box to write in, for textbooks and worksheets. The styles are box, dashed, lines, grid and dots. The rows are how tall it is (4 by default), and the label is optional. ::blank{6} is a six-row box. {box 3 Try it yourself} {lines 4 Write your answer} {grid 4} {dots 3} {dashed 3 Sketch it here} Blanks inside a sentence [ 8] puts a blank to write in right inside a sentence, 8 characters wide. Leave the number out for a standard width. Add an answer after a bar, like [ 8 photosynthesis] , and it stays hidden until you click the blank (it never prints). Plants make food by [ 14 photosynthesis] using [ 6] and water. [ 6] is the same blank drawn as a small empty box instead of a line, and it takes an answer too, like [ 6 2024] . The war ended in [ 6 1945] and began in [ 6].

::pagenumbers{style start} is a small marker that changes how page numbers look from the page it sits on, until the next marker. The styles are none (front matter, no number), arabic , roman (i, ii, iii), upper-roman (I, II, III), alpha (a, b, c), upper-alpha , greek (α, β, γ) and upper-greek . The start number is optional and defaults to 1, so ::pagenumbers{roman 1} starts a Roman section and ::pagenumbers{arabic 1} starts the main text again at 1. Writeout and Bitbook show the numbers on their page sheets (turn on Page Numbers), and the marker itself never prints. In Writeout and Bitbook, use Layout Pages Page Number Format (or View in Bitbook) to place one at the caret!

Poolside Keydown is a dialect of Keydown written for Waterflow, with its own marks and forty original chips. Write it anywhere with the ;;pk{ } block, for example ;;pk{ } inside a sentence. The full reference is in [[poolside-keydown]], and the look behind it is the [[poolside-style Poolside style]].

BitLang BitLang is the small language behind Bitbook programs. A program can show text with renderRT , add buttons with btn , react to keys and the mouse, play beeps, draw with ink, and change how things look with effect size , effect tint and friends. It also runs inside Omicron pages! You add a program to a note with the Programs skill in Bitbook (Skills tab). Press the pencil on the chip to edit it, and click the chip to run it. The guide below is the same one that opens from Bitbook's BitLang Guide button, so it always matches the real language! Programs and View mode A running program is part of the page. Typing in the page or switching modes rebuilds it, which stops the program. Let it run in View mode and keep your hands off the text while it plays!

BitLang is a tiny language for making little programs and games inside Bitbook notes (and Omicron pages). Add a Programs skill to a note and it becomes a chip, just like a BeepBox song: press ✎ on the chip to edit the code, and click the chip to play! While a program plays it takes over the whole document (text, buttons and songs), and the ■ Stop button at the top-right (or Esc) brings your document back. Bitbook is the editor; the same chip also plays in Omicron.

fn onstart(): renderRT(" Y Hello Y from BitLang !", line "1") fn onstart(): runs once when the program starts. Indentation (4 spaces) shows what belongs to a function, an if or a loop, like in Python.

var best 0 saved between plays (great for high scores!) var temp score 0 temporary: starts fresh every play score score + 1 score + 1 var name "Ava" var pos {x: 10, y: 20} a map var items [1, 2, 3] a list var keeps its value after you stop, and comes back next time you play. var temp is reset on every play. Values: numbers, "text" , true / false , null , lists [ ] , maps { } . A bare link is text: var song https://example.com/ abc Comments start with .

fn add(a, b 1): return a + b fn onstart(): once, when the program starts fn onframe(dt): about 60 times a second while it plays; dt seconds since the last frame fn onkey(k): a key goes down ("a", "arrowleft", "space"...) fn onkeyup(k): a key goes up fn onend(): when the program stops In the code editor, Tab indents to the next step of 4 spaces, Shift+Tab takes one step away, and inside the indentation Backspace , Delete and the arrow keys treat each 4 spaces as one tab. Call a function with add(2, 3) or by name: add(2, b 5) . onframe only changes the document ( renderRT , print , buttons...). Rewriting the same text is free, so a clock or a counter can update every frame: var temp t 0 fn onframe(dt): t + dt renderRT("Seconds: " + floor(t) + " ", line "1")

if score 10: print("Great!") elif score 5: print("Nice") else: print("Keep going") while lives 0: lives - 1 for i in range(5): 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 print(i) for item in items: print(item) break continue pass return Operators: + - / % , comparisons ! < > < > , and or not , and in ( 3 in items ). Text + anything joins: "Score " + score .

key("ArrowLeft") true while that key is held ( key("a") , key("space") ) beep(freq, ms) A little square-wave beep remvar(name) Removes a var temp variable (give its name, like remvar(score) ). Using it afterwards is an error until you create it again with var temp . Saved var variables can't be removed! stop() End the program time() Seconds since you pressed Play

print(a, b, ...) Adds a line of plain text renderRT(html, line "1") Shows rich text on a numbered line. line "2" takes over line 2, replacing whatever was written there before (by renderRT , a quick command, or print ). Leave line out and it adds the next free line instead (the same statement keeps its own line, so a loop or onframe updates it in place). It understands HTML and Keydown: Y gel Y , bold , C chip … Where Poolside Keydown is loaded (Bitbook, Waterflow, Writeout, OpenDB), a part of the text can be written in it with ;;pk{ ... } , like renderRT("Score: ;;pk{ <tip Nice!> }") (use single quotes for any quotes inside). ink("gel:red:9:M10 10L80 40") Draws on the program's page with Bitbook's Annotate inks, over everything else. The easy way: press ✏️ Draw in the editor, draw, and press Done : the drawing goes into your code as an @@ink "strokes '...'" line, which runs just like ink(...) ! wait(2) Pauses the program for that many seconds ( wait(0.5) is half a second), then carries on with the next line! It works on a line of its own: at the top level, in onstart , buttons, keys, and functions of your own called on their own line. A while true: loop with a wait inside never runs out of time, and Stop ends the waiting. inkc() Clears the ink : every drawing made with ink(...) (or an @@ink line) leaves the page. Draw again any time with ink(...) ! renderPT(text, line "1

h: BBML: set up the page without renderRT
x: BBML is a little markup (it looks like HTML) for a program's starting page . In the ✎ editor, switch the BitLang BBML button to write it. When the program plays, the BBML lines appear first (right after your top-level code), then onstart runs and keeps adding lines after them. <!-- comments look like this --> <line>Welcome, {name} ! Next year you are {age + 1}.</line> A loose line of text becomes its own line too. <row> <btn do "start"> G Start </btn> <btn do "stop"> R Exit </btn> </row> <line>Name: <textbox var "name">Your name</textbox> Age: <counter var "age" min "0" max "120"/></line> <line n "9"><annotate type "bubble" color "pink">Line 9, in a bubble</annotate></line> <pt>Plain text: these stars stay </pt> <line>…</line> <row> One line of rich text (Keydown works). n "9" puts it on line 9. Everything inside, buttons included, sits on that one line. {expression} Any BitLang expression, worked out when the page is set up: {name} , {age + 1} , {upper(name)} . Write { for a real brace and < for a real <. <btn do "fn">…</btn> A button that runs a function (or stop , or do "lam(...)" ). Its contents are what it looks like. <textbox var "x">hint</textbox> A textbox tied to a variable ( value "..." to start with te

fn onstart(): renderRT("first") no line: takes the next free line (1) renderRT("second") line 2 renderRT("OVERRIDDEN", line 1) line 1 now says OVERRIDDEN annotate bubble("quick commands count as lines too") line 3 print("so does print") line 4 Every piece of output sits on a numbered line, in order. renderRT("text", line N) always replaces line N, even when it has been written on already, so you can redraw one line (a score, a status) without touching the rest. Without line , a new line is added at the end.

h: Rows: several things on one line
x: End a line with & and the next line joins it, so quick commands and buttons sit side by side. They can be stacked as long as you like: fn onstart(): btn(submit, renderRT(" C Submit ")) & btn(stop, renderRT(" R Exit ")) & btn(go, renderRT(" G Go ")) fn submit(): renderRT("Submitted!", line 9) fn go(): renderRT("Going!", line 9) The three buttons appear in one row (one output line). & also works inside renderRT(...) to join text pieces, and the next component can be indented however you like. The last line of a row has no & .

h: onhover: change what shows when the mouse is over it
x: Give btn , renderRT or renderPT an onhover and its contents are swapped for the new ones while the mouse is over it (it keeps the room for both, so nothing jumps around). The hover contents are Keydown too, like renderRT(" Hi ", onhover " Y Bye Y ") , and can be a renderRT(...) result as well. Inside renderPT they stay plain text, no Keydown. The swap fades (add transition 0 to make it instant), and the hover contents can hold effects , like onhover effect size("Play", 1.3) to grow while the mouse is over it: fn onstart(): renderRT(btn(go, " C Play ", onhover " G Let's go! "), line "1") renderRT("Move the mouse here", onhover " Hello! Y Nice to meet you Y ", line "2") renderPT("Plain text", onhover " stars stay stars", line "3") renderRT(hover(btn(go, "Open"), "Opens the door"), line "4") hover(contents, onhover) works on anything fn go(): print("clicked") In BBML, write onhover "..." on <btn> , <pt> , <line> , <row> or <span> , like <btn do "go" onhover " G Go! "> C Play </btn> .

h: Effects: saturation, brightness, blur and more
x: An effect wraps text with Keydown formatting, or an element like a button or a text box, and changes how it looks. Everything outside it stays as it is: fn onstart(): renderRT(effect saturation("++R+Text++ ", 0) + "Normal text") the red chip turns gray renderRT(effect blur(" soft words", 1.5) + " and sharp ones") renderRT(effect grayscale(btn(go, " G Go "), 1) & btn(go, " G Go ")) an element: the first button turns gray renderRT(effect brightness(effect hue("++B+Hue turned++", 120), 1.4)) effects can sit inside each other fn go(): print("clicked") effect saturation(x, n) 0 is gray, 1 is normal, 2 is extra vivid. effect brightness(x, n) 0 is black, 1 is normal, 2 is twice as bright. effect contrast(x, n) 0 is flat gray, 1 is normal, 2 is punchy. effect grayscale(x, n) effect sepia(x, n) effect invert(x, n) 0 is normal, 1 is fully gray, brown or flipped. effect hue(x, degrees) Turns every color around the color wheel. effect blur(x, pixels) Makes it soft. effect opacity(x, n) 0 is invisible, 1 is normal. effect tint(x, color, n) Colors it, like a colored glass over it: the light and dark parts stay. The color is a name ( "red" , "slate" ), a number 1 to 13 (like annotate), " 336699" or "rgb(51, 102, 153)" . n is how strong, from 0 (the original) to 1 (all the way, the default). effect size(x, n, seconds) Makes it bigger or smaller: 1 is normal, 1.5 is half as big again, 0.5 i

A lambda is a little function written in one place. Put statements inside lam(...) , separated by ; , and keep it in a variable (or hand it straight to a button): var done lam(renderRT("Good job! You did it", line 1); btn(stop, renderRT(" R Exit ")) &; btn(submit, renderRT(" G Submit "))) fn onstart(): done() runs every statement, in order fn later(): btn(lam(renderPT("clicked", line 5); beep(660, 80)), " C Click me ") a lambda as a button's function Each ; starts the next statement, exactly like a new line. A & right before a ; keeps the next statement on the same line of output (the & row rule), so the Exit and Submit buttons sit side by side. A lambda takes no values. It sees your variables, and return works inside it.

ls set(key, value) Saves a number, text, true/false, list or map under a name. It is still there next time (even after closing the page). ls get(key, default) Reads it back (or default , or null , when nothing is saved). ls remove(key) Forgets one key. ls keys() A list of every key this program saved. ls clear() Forgets all of this program's keys. to json(x) from json(text, default) Turn a list/map into text and back (handy with files). var temp visits ls get("visits", 0) fn onstart(): ls set("visits", visits + 1) renderPT("You have been here " + (visits + 1) + " times", line 1) Every program has its own private shelf. Add shared true (like ls get("name", "", shared true) ) to use a shelf all programs share. ( var variables are also saved for you, but ls gives you named keys, lists and maps.)

export file(name, text) Saves a text file to the person's computer (their browser downloads it). import file(fn) Opens the file picker. When a file is chosen, fn(name, text) runs with its name and text. Add accept ".csv,.json" to limit the types. Files up to 1 MB. fn onstart(): btn(pick, " C Open a file ") & btn(save, " G Save a file ") fn pick(): import file(got) fn got(name, text): renderPT(name + " has " + len(text) + " letters", line 3) fn save(): export file("hello.txt", "Hello from BitLang!") The browser only opens the picker (or a download) after a click, so call these from a button's function. Programs can only read a file the person picks, and only save through a normal download.

regex test(pattern, text) true if the pattern is found anywhere in the text. regex match(pattern, text) The first match as a map ( m.text , m.index , m.groups the (...) parts, m.named for (?<name>...) parts) or null . regex all(pattern, text) A list of every match (add full true for maps like regex match). regex replace(pattern, text, with) Replaces every match. $1 in with is the first (...) part. regex split(pattern, text) Cuts the text at each match into a list. regex test("^[A-Z]", "Hello") true regex all("\d+", "a1 b22 c333") ["1", "22", "333"] regex replace("(\w+)@(\w+)", "me@site", "$2/$1") "site/me" regex match("(?<y>\d{4})-(\d\d)", "on 2026-10").named.y "2026" Patterns work like JavaScript's. Write a backslash twice inside quotes ( "\d" for a digit). Add flags "i" to ignore case (also m , s ). Patterns up to 500 letters and texts up to 200,000 letters; a bad pattern shows a plain error.

A button runs one of your functions when someone clicks it. You need two things: a function that says what happens, and a btn(...) that puts a clickable thing on the page. 1. The smallest button fn onstart(): btn(hello, "Click me") fn hello(): renderRT("You clicked it! Y Hooray Y ", line "2") btn(hello, "Click me") has two parts : first the function's name, then what the button looks like. Write the function name without brackets : hello , not hello() . With brackets you would run it right now instead of giving it to the button. On a line of its own, btn(...) shows itself. Inside other text, use renderRT (see 3). 2. A button that changes something (a counter) var temp clicks 0 fn onstart(): draw() fn draw(): renderRT("Clicks: " + clicks + " " + btn(add, " C +1 "), line "1") fn add(): clicks + 1 draw() A button's function takes no values , so keep what you need in a var or var temp (here clicks ). Pressing the button changes clicks , then draw() writes the same line again with the new number. Writing a line again replaces it, so the button stays in place. 3. Buttons inside text, and several at once fn onstart(): renderRT("Pick one: " + btn(red, "Red") + " " + btn(blue, "Blue"), line "1") fn red(): renderRT("You picked red !", line "2") fn blue(): renderRT("You picked blue !", line "2") Join buttons with + and text, like any other text. Each btn needs its own function. 4. Make th

While a program plays, the page can't be edited, so nobody can change your text by accident. The exceptions are boxes you add yourself: var name "" var temp age 0 fn onstart(): renderRT("Name: " + textbox("Type your name", variable name), line "1") renderRT("Age: " + counter(variable age, min 0, max 120), line "2") renderRT(btn(hello, " C Say hi "), line "3") fn hello(): renderRT("Hi " + name + " , you are " + age + "!", line "4") textbox(placeholder, variable x) A box to type in. variable x (no quotes) updates the variable while the person types . The short form textbox("Text here", x) does the same. The placeholder is the dimmed hint; it understands Keydown and skills ( textbox(annotate box("Name")) , even songs). value "..." sets what it starts with. counter(variable x, min 0, max 10) (Short form: counter(x) .) A smaller box for numbers only (digits, one dot, a leading minus). The variable gets a real number. Empty counts as 0. min and max are applied when the person leaves the box. It takes a placeholder too, but no Keydown typing. People can type Keydown into a textbox ( bold , Y gel Y ), but the variable gets its plain text ("bold", "gel"). They cannot add skills: anything typed is only text. A variable only changes when the text really changed, so typing stays smooth. If your program changes the variable ( name "" ), the box shows the new value. Create the variable with

var temp song https://ultraabox.github.io/ u5N0btuff... fn onstart(): renderRT(skill(skill "beepbox", get song, content inherit) + "", line "1") skill(skill "beepbox", get link, content inherit) builds a BeepBox song player. content inherit means the song data is taken from the link itself ( inherit only works with the BeepBox skill ). Add label "My song" to name the chip. In Bitbook the chip plays the song; in Omicron it opens the link.

renderRT("Look: " + skill(skill "annotate", type "bubble", color "pink", content renderRT("Some totally random text here")), line "1") skill(skill "annotate", type ..., color ..., content ...) wraps text in one of Bitbook's Annotate highlights. content can be renderRT("...") : used inside another call, renderRT just hands back its rich text instead of showing it. type is highlight , underline , strikethrough , box , halo , brackets , spotlight , accent , bubble or one of the colorful ones: dusk prism complement ticket neon stamp tape checker halftone aurora mild (pale versions of every color) wrap belt bucket torpedo bottle packet select capsule frost pixel flag gem . color (default yellow ) is red, orange, gold, yellow, lime, green, turquoise, teal, cyan, blue, purple, pink or slate. Annotate highlights make great btn contents!

The long skill(...) forms have short versions: annotate bubble("Some totally cool text here", color 1) The same as skill(skill "annotate", type "bubble", color ..., content ...) . There is one for every type: annotate highlight annotate underline annotate strikethrough annotate box annotate halo annotate brackets annotate spotlight annotate accent annotate bubble and annotate dusk annotate prism annotate complement annotate ticket annotate neon annotate stamp annotate tape annotate checker annotate halftone annotate aurora annotate mild annotate wrap annotate belt annotate bucket annotate torpedo annotate bottle annotate packet annotate select annotate capsule annotate frost annotate pixel annotate flag annotate gem color 1 … color 13 Colors by number: 1 red, 2 orange, 3 gold, 4 yellow, 5 lime, 6 green, 7 turquoise, 8 teal, 9 cyan, 10 blue, 11 purple, 12 pink, 13 slate. Names work too: color "pink" , or put it second: annotate box("text", "blue") beepbox(link, label "My song") The same as skill(skill "beepbox", get link, content inherit) On a line of their own they show themselves right away. Inside renderRT(...) you can mix them with other text: annotate bubble("Some totally cool text here", color 1) renderRT("Hi " + annotate box("there", "blue") + " " + beepbox(song), line "9")

len(x) How many items / letters push(list, x) pop(list) remove(list, x) Change a list list[0] list[-1] map.key map["key"] Read (or set) a slot; a missing one is null range(n) range(a, b) range(a, b, step) Lists of numbers str(x) num(x) join(list, sep) split(text, sep) upper lower contains keys Handy tools

var who "Text" mat Censor: ( "badword" ~ " " "just some text" ~ 1 ) mat Swap: ( "matchme" ~ "replaceme" "a variable" ~ who a value can be a variable who ~ "a variable" and so can what you look for ) fn onstart(): renderRT(mat match("a variable", Swap), line 1) Text renderRT(mat match("no badword here", Censor), line 2) no here renderPT(mat match("just some text", Censor), line 3) 1 mat Name: ( ... ) makes a matcher: one "what to find" ~> what it becomes per line (commas are fine too, and comments work inside). mat match(x, Name) : if x is exactly one of the keys, you get its value (any kind: text, a number, a list...). Otherwise, if x is text, every key found inside it is swapped (longest first). Swapping happens once : a replacement is never matched again, so "a variable" becomes "Text" and stays "Text" even though "Text" is also a key. Keys and values are read when you match, so they always use the variables' current values. mat match(list, Name) matches every item. mat has(x, Name) is true when anything matched, and mat keys(Name) lists the keys. Change a pair with matc and the mouse operator "> : matc Censor ["badword" ~> " "] "> ["badword" ~> "(oops)"] . The first [...] is the pair as it is now (key and value), the second is what it becomes. The new key and value are read right then. Not to be confused with mat(...) , which makes a matrix: a matcher is mat ,

var v < 1, 2, 3 > a vector: < numbers, separated by commas > var m [1 2; 3 4] a matrix: numbers with spaces, ; starts a new row var id identity(2) [1 0; 0 1] Vector < 1, 2, 3 > (or vec(1, 2, 3) ). Read parts with v[0] or v.x v.y v.z v.w , count with v.length or len(v) , change with v[1] 9 or v[1] + 5 , and loop with for x in v: . Matrix [1 2; 3 4] (or mat([[1, 2], [3, 4]]) ). Spaces separate the numbers, so use brackets for sums: [(1 + 2) 4] , and [1 -2] is two numbers. m[1] is a row (a live vector), m[1][0] one number, m.rows m.cols and m.T (the transpose) work. [1, 2; 3, 4] with commas is fine too, and then each part can be a full sum. Plain [1, 2, 3] with commas and no ; is still a normal list. v + w v - w Add or subtract vectors (or matrices) of the same size. v 2 2 v v / 2 Scale. A number with + or - goes into every slot. v w Vectors multiply slot by slot. For the dot product use dot(v, w) . m n m v m 3 Matrix times matrix, matrix times vector (the vector stands up as a column), and matrix power. dot(v, w) cross(v, w) norm(v) normalize(v) Dot product, cross product (3 numbers each), length, and the same direction with length 1. det(m) inverse(m) transpose(m) trace(m) Determinant, inverse, transpose, and the sum of the diagonal. identity(n) zeros(n) zeros(r, c) The identity matrix, a vector of zeros, and a matrix of zeros. rows(m) cols(m) to list(x) Sizes,

h: Libraries: use python, use sqlite, use lua
x: Put use lines at the very top of your program to load a library. They load before the program starts (you will see a loading message the first time). use sqlite use python use python numpy, pandas extra Python packages from Pyodide's list use lua python(code) (Pyodide) use python fn onstart(): var temp total python("sum(range(10)) k", k 2) 90 renderPT("total " + total, line 1) python("import math\nroots [math.sqrt(x) for x in range(4)]") renderPT(to json(python("roots")), line 2) variables stay for the next python() call python("print('hello from Python')") prints show up as lines python("code") runs the code and gives back the value of its last expression (numbers, text, true/false, None null , lists, and dicts become maps). Extra name value pieces become Python variables first ( k 2 above). Python keeps its variables between calls while the program runs. Errors show the Python message and the line of your BitLang program. The first run downloads Pyodide (about 10 MB) from the internet; after that it is cached by the browser. Python is more powerful than BitLang , so the first time you play a program that uses it you are asked to Allow it (you can tick "Always allow this exact program"). Suave Suave is a smooth, readable programming language for scripts, data and web apps. It runs in the terminal on Deno and in the browser, and it comes with a big standard library: 59 modules and about 1,050 functions , including parsers and writers for JSON, YAML, TOML, CSV, XML, INI and SUVL , Suave's own data format. It also has complex and imaginary numbers , quantum computing and quantum mechanics , pools (values that are decided when they are used), async/await , and a built-in package manager . Suave looks like Python: colons, indentation, def, elif, lambda, class use std.json use std.table class Dog: name: str age: num 1 def speak(self): return f"{self.name} is {self.age} and says woof!" def describe(n): if n % 15 0: return "FizzBuzz" elif n % 3 0: return "Fizz" else: return str(n) print(Dog("Rex").speak()) print([describe(n) for n in range(1, 8)]) people json.parse('[{"name": "Ada", "age": 36}, {"name": "Bob", "age": 25}]') table.from(people).sort by("age", desc True).print() Suave also has Lake (a task runner: a Lakefile with tasks, like Make or Rake) and Laker (desktop apps from a Suave web app, like Tauri), see docs/LAKE.md and docs/LAKER.md. Examples to read: examples/pdf-annotator/ (a PDF annotator) and examples/keydown-editor/ (a Keydown editor), both one Suave file plus a plain index.html . Suave files come in three kinds: .sv (programs and modules), .xsv (web c

Suave aims at the everyday jobs people reach for Python, R, Julia, Clojure or Rust for, in one small language: You might use for In Suave --- --- --- Python scripts, glue, quick tools suave run , a REPL, std.fs , std.process , std.cli , readable code R / pandas tables and statistics std.table , std.stats , std.plot (terminal charts and SVG) Julia / NumPy numbers and matrices std.math , std.linalg , std.bigint , std.rational , std.complex Clojure data pipelines, lazy sequences \ pipes, std.iter , std.func (compose, curry, memoize, trampoline) Rust enums, pattern matching, Result and ? , traits all of those, plus type annotations that are checked as the program runs Qiskit / QuTiP quantum circuits and quantum mechanics std.quantum (a state-vector simulator with Grover, Shor, teleportation) and std.qm (Schrodinger solver, hydrogen, spin) npm / pip / cargo packages suave add , suave install , a lock file with checksums, registries that are just folders JavaScript web apps runs in the browser; std.dom has a small state / view / update framework It is a young project (version 0.1), written in JavaScript so it runs anywhere Deno or a browser does. See Where Suave is today for the honest limits.

The quickest way: paste this one line into Terminal. It downloads Suave, checks the download, installs Deno if you need it, and sets everything up: curl -fsSL https://radii-office.com/suave/install.sh sh Run the same line again, or type suave upgrade , to get the newest version. To remove it: ~/.suave/install.sh --uninstall . Already have this folder? Open Terminal in it and run: ./install.sh (Or double-click Install Suave.command in Finder.) It installs Deno if you do not have it, puts the commands suave , lake and laker in ~/.local/bin , and makes sure new terminal windows can find them. Open a new terminal window afterwards and try suave eval "1 + 2" . If macOS says a file "cannot be opened because it is from an unidentified developer", the installer already clears that for this folder; if it still stops you, right-click the file and choose Open once. To remove everything again: ./install.sh --uninstall . Without installing: deno run -A bin/suave.js run hello.sv , or deno task suave run hello.sv . Windows: install Deno, then use deno task install .

x: use std.quantum as q use std.async // complex numbers are part of the language print((3 + 4i) (1 - 2i), sqrt(-4)) // 11 - 2i 2i // a quantum computer let bell q.register(2).h(0).cx(0, 1) print(bell, bell.sample(100)) // 0.7071 00 + 0.7071 11 {"00": 52, "11": 48} print(q.shor(21).factors) // [3, 7] // a pool is decided when it is first used let weather pool ["rain", "sun"] let plans [weather, weather] // still undecided print("It will be {weather}") // decided now, and it stays // async and await async fn slow(x) { await async.delay(0.1); x 2 } print(await async.all([slow(1), slow(2), slow(3)])) // [2, 4, 6] in 0.1 s, not 0.3 suave add mathx install a package (and what it needs), with a lock file suave publish --to ./reg publish your own to a registry folder Guides: docs/QUANTUM.md, docs/POOLS.md, docs/PM.md.

Honest notes for version 0.1: It is an interpreter written in JavaScript. On this Mac, fib(30) takes about 0.26 s (CPython 3.13: about 0.1 s) and a 3-million-step loop about 0.25 s (CPython: 0.3 s). Fine for scripts, data work, small servers and web apps; not for heavy number crunching. async/await is built in, and the older callback style still works ( http.get(url, res ...) , time.after(1, f) ). Tasks take turns on one thread (like JavaScript); there are no threads. Quantum is a simulator on a normal computer: up to 22 qubits, no noise. Types are checked while the program runs , not before. Annotations like fn f(x: int) - str are enforced at the call. Packages: the package manager works with folders, tarballs, GitHub and registry folders, but there is no official public registry yet. // starts a comment , so whole-number division is div(7, 2) (or 7.div(2) ). Deep recursion works to about 90,000 calls with the bin/suave launcher (about 8,000 with plain deno run ). Tested on macOS with Deno 2.9 and Chrome. Firefox, Safari and Windows have not been tried yet.

The Suave language A guide to every part of the language. Code blocks run as shown with suave run .

Suave reads like Python, with a few things made easier. A line that ends with a colon opens a block of the lines indented below it: a comment def grade(score): if score 90: return "A" elif score 80: return "B" else: return "keep going" total 0 for i in range(1, 4): total + i print(grade(85), total) What is the same as Python: def , if / elif / else , for x in items: , while , lambda x: x 2 , value if condition else other , True / False / None , and / or / not / in , pass , try / except / finally , raise , import math , from math import sqrt, pi , a, b b, a , first, rest items , for key, value in pairs: , f"..." , sum(x for x in xs) and f(size 3) . What is easier: No init . A class lists its fields and def methods: class Dog: then name: str , age: num 1 , def speak(self): ... . Make one with Dog("Rex") or Dog(name "Rex") . Plain x 5 makes a changeable variable (and x 6 later changes it, even from inside a function). Write let x 5 when it should be locked. match takes case lines: case 1 2: , case n if n 100: , case : . Only false and none are false, so 0 , "" and [] do not surprise you, and // stays a comment (floor division is div(a, b) ). Both styles work and can be mixed: fn f(x) { x + 1 } is the same as def f(x): return x + 1 . The rest of this page shows the original brace style next to it; every example works either way.

a Python-style comment suave // a line comment (still works) / a block comment, / which can nest / / A statement ends at the end of the line (or at ; ). A line carries on when it ends inside ( ) or [ ] , or when the next line starts with .method , , ?? , and or or : suave let total [1, 2, 3] .map( x x 2) .sum()

let name "Ada" print("Hello, {name}! {1 + 2} {[1, 2].len()}") // {expression} inside "..." is interpolated print('no {interpolation} in single quotes') // '...' is plain (escapes still work) print(r"C:\path\no escapes") // r"..." is raw print(""" several lines, dedented to the least indented line """) print("a \{ brace \} and a tab:\t.") print("{3.14159:.2f} {255:x} {42: 8} {"hi":^8} {1234567:,} {0.256:.1%}") // format specs after a colon Regular expressions and braces: \d{4} inside "..." looks like an interpolation. Write patterns as r"\d{4}" or '\d{4}' . Format spec: [fill][align< ^ ][sign][ ][0][width][,][.precision][type] with types d f e x X o b % . Text is indexed by character: s[0] , s[-1] , s[1..3] , s[..2] , s[3..] .

let x 1 // cannot be reassigned var y 2 // can: y 3, y + 1 const LIMIT 10 let [first, ..rest] [1, 2, 3] let {name, age: years} {name: "Ada", age: 36} var (a, b) (1, 2) (a, b) (b, a) // swap Compound assignment: + - / % ?? .

From loosest to tightest: , ?? , or , and , not / ! , comparisons ( ! in not in is is not ), range .. .. , + - , / % , unary - , (right to left), then .member ?.member [i] (call) ? . - / always divides exactly ( 7 / 2 is 3.5 ); use div(7, 2) for whole-number division. Dividing by zero is an error. - % takes the sign of the right side ( -7 % 3 is 2 ). - + joins text, lists, tuples, maps (right side wins) and sets (union); repeats text and lists; - on sets is a difference. - compares by value (lists, maps, structs, enums). - a ?? b is b only when a is none . - x f(y) is f(x, y) ; x f is f(x) . - x?.name gives none if x is none, and the rest of the chain is skipped too. - x is int , x is none , x is Point test types; x in coll tests membership.

fn add(a, b 10) a + b // body for one expression fn many(first, rest) { [first, rest.len()] } fn area(w: num, h: num) - num { w h } // checked when called add(1) // 11 add(b: 5, a: 1) // named arguments, any order many(1, 2, 3) // [1, 2] many( [7, 8, 9]) // spread a list into arguments let twice f x f(f(x)) // lambdas and closures fn counter() { var n 0; { n + 1; n } } - The last expression is the result; return leaves early. - Functions can be used before they are written in the same file. - Too few or too many arguments is an error (lambdas ignore extras).

Fill in some values now and give the rest later! Put where a value is still missing, or use partial : fn sub(a, b) a - b fn greet(hello, name, punct ".") hello + ", " + name + punct let from10 sub(10, ) // a new function waiting for b from10(3) // 7 let minus1 sub( , 1) // waiting for a [5, 6].map(sub( , 1)) // [4, 5] 5 sub(100, ) // 95 (the piped value lands in the ) let add1 partial(add, 1) // the first value is fixed partial right(sub, 1)(10) // 9 (fixed values go on the end) let hi partial(greet, "Hello", punct "!") // named values work too hi("Sam") // "Hello, Sam!" add.partial(7)(1) // functions have .partial and .partial right too is partial(hi) // true - Several are filled left to right, and extra values go on the end. - Giving fewer values than there are is an ArgError that says how many are still missing. - Values and named arguments are worked out once, when the partial function is made.

Everything is an expression: let size if n 100 { "big" } else if n 10 { "mid" } else { "small" } for i in 0..10 { if i % 2 0 { continue }; if i 7 { break } } for (i, ch) in "abc".chars().enumerate() { print(i, ch) } for (key, value) in {a: 1, b: 2} { print(key, value) } var n 0 while n 10 { break n } } // break can carry a value

match value { 0 "zero", 1 2 3 "small", 4..10 "medium", // 4 up to but not including 10 n if n 100 "huge {n}", // a guard "hi" "greeting", [] "empty", [x] "one {x}", [first, ..rest] "{first} then {rest.len()} more", {kind: "circle", r} "circle {r}", // maps and structs {name, ..others} "{name} and {others.len()} more keys", (a, b) "pair", // tuples; [..] fits only lists in a match Circle(r) "circle", // enum variants and structs, by name none "nothing", "anything else" } A match that fits nothing is an error. The same patterns work after let , in for , and in function parameters.

3i is an imaginary number, so 3 + 4i is a complex one. They work with + - / , with ordinary numbers, and with sqrt , abs and the std.math functions: let z 3 + 4i print(z z, abs(z), z.conj(), z.re, z.im) // -7 + 24i 5 3 - 4i 3 4 print(sqrt(-4), 1i 2) // 2i -1 + 0i

A pool is a value that is decided when it is first used, then stays decided: let coin pool ["heads", "tails"] let plans [coin, coin] // not decided yet print("It is {coin}") // decided now; every use after this agrees pool 1.. 6 , pool {"a": 3, "b": 1} (weights), pool sampler() . See POOLS.md.

use std.async async fn price(item) { await async.delay(0.1) // wait without blocking anything {item, cost: 5} } let a await price("apple") // one at a time let all await async.all([price("pear"), price("plum")]) // at the same time print(a, all) - async fn and async x ... make functions that give back a future ; await waits for one. async { ... } is an async block that runs right away and gives a future. - Calling an async function starts it at once (like JavaScript). await can be used inside an async function and at the top of a program (or a test block), and not inside a normal function. - await works inside if , match , for , while , loop , try/catch/finally , strings ( "{await f()}" ), lists, maps and calls. Awaiting a plain value gives it back. - A future that fails throws when awaited, so try { await f() } catch e { ... } works. A failure nobody awaited is reported at the end. - std.async has all race any settle timeout retry map limit deferred channel lock semaphore spawn delay ; http.fetch(url) , time.delay(s) and process.exec(cmd, args) give futures. Futures have .then(f) , .catch(f) and .finally(f) . - Only code that really contains an await is slowed down; everything else runs as before.

try { risky() } catch e { print("failed: {e.message}") } finally { cleanup() } throw "any value can be thrown" try { throw {code: 7} } catch {code} { print(code) } // Result: Ok(value) or Err(reason), and ? passes an Err (or none) up fn read(path) { let text fs.read(path); Ok(text) } parse(s).map( n n 2).unwrap or(0) match parse(s) { Ok(n) n, Err(e) 0 } A caught runtime error is a map with kind , message and line . assert , assert eq , assert ne , assert throws , panic .

use std.dom dom.text(dom.query(" root"), "Hello from Suave!") suave.js is the whole language and standard library in one file (about 280 KB). Build it with deno task bundle (it lands in dist/suave.js ), or let suave build do it. Opening a page from disk (file://) works too: browsers will not let such a page read other files, so write a twin beside each Suave file it loads with suave twin app.wsv components/counter.xsv (it makes app.wsv.js , which a plain can load). Suave finds the twins by itself, including the files a page brings in with use "./counter.xsv" . suave build app.wsv already puts everything inside index.html , so it needs no twins. Several tags share one scope, in order. src "app.sv" loads a file. A tag with data-module "util.sv" is not run; it is a module for use "./util.sv" . print writes to the browser console, and also into an element with id "suave-output" if the page has one. A program error shows in a red box at the bottom of the page, with the line and source. From JavaScript: Suave.run(code) and Suave.eval(code) .

h: The easy web (std.web): start here if websites are new to you
x: You do not need to know HTML, callbacks or promises. use std.web gives plain words for the common jobs: use std.web 1. Start a website with one line (a page, a folder, or several addresses) web.serve(web.page("Hello", web.h1("Welcome!"), web.p("This is my first site."))) web.serve("public") share a folder web.serve({"/": " Home ", "/time": time.now(), "POST /save": req {got: req.json}}) web.serve( req "Hello from " + req.path) answer every address 2. Read things from the web (put await in front) let text await web.get("https://example.com") let data await web.json("https://api.example.com/items") let reply await web.post("https://api.example.com/save", {name: "Sam"}) if await web.is up("https://example.com"): print("it works!") 3. Build pages with words instead of tags (your text is made safe for you) web.page("Shop", web.h1("Today's fruit"), web.list(["apple", "pear"]), web.table([["apple", 3], ["pear", 5]], ["Fruit", "Price"]), web.p("See ", web.link("our map", "https://example.com/map"))) 4. In a browser page: put things on screen, one word each web.heading("Greeter") web.input("Your name", name web.say("Hello " + name + "!")) web.button("Click me", web.say("Clicked!")) web.get web.json web.post web.put web.delete give back the answer, and a failure says what went wrong ( 404 Not Found ). web.is up(url) and web.status(url) never fail. web.page h1 h2 h3 p bold italic code quo

web.page comes with a clean built-in look (readable text, tidy tables, round buttons, a .box class). To change it you add CSS, and there are four ways, from easiest to most flexible: use std.web 1. Write the CSS as a map (no braces or semicolons to get wrong). Use for dashes: font size is font-size. let look web.css({ ".card": {border: "2px solid teal", padding: "1rem", border radius: "12px"}, "h1": {color: "teal"} }) 2. Give things a class with web.div / web.span, then style the class let card web.div("card", web.h2("Today"), web.p("Sunny!")) 3. Or style one thing right where it is let note web.styled("color: crimson; font-size: 1.4rem", "Careful!") 4. Hand the sheet to the page (it comes after the built-in look, so yours wins) web.serve(web.page("My site", web.h1("Hello"), card, note, css: look)) You can also write the sheet as plain text, css: 'h1 { color: teal }' , and web.style(sheet) makes a you can put inside any part of a page. Use single quotes (or r"..." ) around CSS text. Inside normal double quotes Suave treats { } as a value to fill in, so "h1 { color: red }" is an error. web.css({...}) avoids the problem completely. In a browser, web.add css(sheet) adds a style sheet to the live page, and web.div / web.styled pieces can be placed on it with web.say ktext or dom.html . h: More sounds: noise, chip noise, harmonics, FM and superchip
x: await sound.noise(1, 0.3) white noise: seconds, volume (color: "pink" or "brown" for softer noise; seed 1 repeats the same noise) await sound.chipnoise(6000, 0.5, 0.3) chip noise: steps per second (higher hissier), seconds, volume await sound.chipnoise(4000, 0.5, 0.3, type "buzz") retro (default), buzz, white, bit, crackle await sound.harmonics(220, 1, 0.4, h [1, 0.5, 0.33, 0.25]) sines at 1x, 2x, 3x, 4x the pitch with these strengths (0 to 1) await sound.harmonics(220, 1, 0.4, h "organ") shapes: sine saw square triangle organ bell await sound.fm(220, 1, 0.4, algorithm 5, ratios [1, 2, 3, 1], levels [15, 9, 4, 0], feedback 3) await sound.superchip(440, 1, 0.4) a bright chip lead Noise: sound.noise (also sound.white ) has no pitch, so it starts with the length. color is white , pink or brown . Chip noise is made the way old game consoles made it: a shift register that is stepped as many times a second as the first number says, so it sounds like a held, steppy hiss. retro is the long register (a hiss that only repeats after 32767 steps), buzz is the short one (a pitched, metallic buzz that repeats every 93 steps), white and bit are random levels, and crackle is rare clicks. Harmonics adds sine waves at whole-number multiples of the pitch. Give a list of strengths (the first is the pitch itself, the second the octave above...) up to 64, or a shape name. Harmonics too high to hear

Six instruments from the UltraBox song "Look at instruments", rebuilt from numbers. They take a pitch in Hz, seconds and a volume, like the waves, and the same named options (an option you give wins over the instrument's own): await sound.high superchip(440, 1) the superchip lead, with a thin 1/8 pulse wave await sound.flute(440, 1) a steady flute: the pitch plus weak odd harmonics, a late vibrato await sound.electric piano(440, 1) FM electric piano (also sound.epiano) await sound.scoot(220, 0.4) a double saw through a ringing low pass that snaps shut: a quick "scoot" await sound.tweet(440, 1) a sine two octaves above the pitch, wobbling heavily and dying away await sound.high scoot(220, 0.4) a scoot made from the spiky wave sound.instruments() the list of their names They also work by name everywhere: sound.make("flute", 440, 1).eq(treble -4).play() , sound.start("scoot", 220, 0.4) . How they were made: I rendered a note of each instrument with UltraBox itself and matched the length, the fade, and the strength of the harmonics (flute, tweet, scoot and high scoot match very closely; the electric piano is close but its 2nd and 4th harmonics are a little off). UltraBox's reverb and stereo panning are not copied. Tweet plays four times the pitch you give (its only harmonic is the 4th), so the pitch can be at most 5000 Hz. Every play function already starts at once; await is what waits for the end. sound.start starts a sound and gives you a Playing straight away: let p sound.start("superchip", 440, 5) the same kinds and options as sound.make print(p.playing()) true sound.start(sound.make("noise", 1, 0.2).lowpass(800)) or start a Sound you built p.stop() end it now await p.wait() or wait for it In a web page sound.start and the play functions play straight from memory with the browser's audio engine, so they begin with no delay. On a Mac, in the terminal, a tiny helper program ( suave-audio-mac , which comes with Suave) is started when you write use std.sound . It keeps the sound card open, so every sound begins within a few thousandths of a second, and sounds that play one after another no longer wait for a new player each time (the Mac's own afplay needs over a second to start, every time). The first sound of a program waits for the helper to wake up (about half a second to one second), so a short script with many sounds is much quicker than before. If the helper cannot start, Suave plays with afplay as before. To always use the old way, set the environment variable SUAVE SLOW SOUND 1 . To rebuild the helper, run sh tools/build-audio-mac.sh (it needs the Swift compiler). sound.melody plays a whole tune from a string of notes, with no gaps and one await : await sound.melody("D F A C+") D, F and A in octave 4, then C one octave up await sound.melody("D F A C+", octave 3, bpm 90, instrument "superchip") await sound.melody("C:2 E G C/E/G:2", reverb 0.3) lengths, bar lines and a chord let tune sound.make melody("D F A C+", octave 4) the same tune as a Sound you can change await tune.lowpass(1200).play() print(sound.note("A4")) 440 (the pitch of a note, in Hz) Notes are the letters C D E F G A B (either case). Add for sharp or b for flat ( F , Bb ). A number after the letter picks the octave for that note ( A5 ); without one the note uses the octave option (default 4, where A is 440 Hz). + goes one octave up and - one down ( C+ , G- , C++ ). Lengths come after a colon in beats ( C:2 is two beats, E:0.5 half a beat). Every note lasts one beat if you give no length. A rest is r (or ) and takes the same :length . Chords join notes with a slash: C/E/G . Bar lines ( ) are just spaces, and you can give a list of notes instead of one string. Options: octave (default 4), bpm (beats a minute, default 120), instrument (any sound kind: sine , square , superchip , flute , scoot ... default sine ), volume (default 0.5), and every note option ( adsr , lowpass , a , r , fade out ...) which goes to each note. reverb , room and damp go over the whole tune once. sound

reverb 0.3 puts a sound in a room (0 is off, 1 is a very wet room). room is the size of the room (0 to 1, default 0.5, a bigger room rings for longer) and damp how soft its walls are (0 to 1, default 0.5, a higher number takes the shine off the echoes): await sound.sine(440, 0.1, reverb 0.5) a short blip in a room await sound.sine(440, 0.1, reverb 0.5, room 1) in a cathedral await sound.make("square", 220, 0.5).reverb(0.4).play() for n in [220, 330, 440, 660] { await sound.sine(n, 0.1, reverb 0.5) } A reverb adds a quiet tail after the sound (up to four seconds in the biggest room). await finishes when the sound itself is over, so the next note starts at once and the tail of the first goes on sounding under it, like in a real room. The program still waits for the very last tail before it ends. reverb 0 (or false ) switches it off.

h: Changing a sound (ADSR, volume, filters, EQ)
x: Add named options to any play function ( sine square triangle mole wave file git mint melody ): await sound.sine(220, 0.5, a 0.05, v 0.4) attack 0.05 s, volume 0.4 await sound.square(220, 1, a 0.02, d 0.1, s 0.6, r 0.3) a full ADSR envelope await sound.sine(440, 1, adsr [0.02, 0.1, 0.6, 0.3]) the same, as a list (or a map {attack: ..., release: ...}) await sound.square(220, 1, lowpass 800) lowpass / highpass / bandpass in Hz (also lp hp bp), q sets the sharpness await sound.triangle(330, 1, eq {bass: 6, mid: 0, treble: -4}) boost or cut in dB await sound.sine(330, 1, eq [[1000, 8], [4000, -6]]) your own bands: [pitch, dB] or [pitch, dB, width] await sound.file("./click.wav", highpass 300, fade out 0.2, v 0.5) ADSR shapes how loud a note is over time: a ttack (seconds to rise to full volume), d ecay (seconds to fall to the sustain level), s ustain (the level it holds, 0 to 1) and r elease (seconds to fade to silence at the end of the sound). Any of a d s r can be left out (they default to 0, 0, 1 and 0). The release happens inside the length you give, so sound.sine(440, 1, r 0.3) fades during its last 0.3 seconds. Volume is v (or volume ), 0 to 1. Filters keep or remove pitches: lowpass lets low sounds through, highpass lets high ones through, bandpass keeps a narrow band around the pitch. EQ ( eq ) turns bass (below about 250 Hz), mid (around 1000 Hz) and treble (above about 40

File What it is How you use it --- --- --- .sv a Suave program or module suave run app.sv , or use "./util.sv" .xsv a web component : props, script, template and style in one file use "./counter.xsv" makes Counter , then in a template .wsv a web page or app : the same parts plus a suave serve app.wsv , suave build app.wsv -o dist Suave is also a small web framework, and it is made so that someone new to websites can use it. The easy style has no tags to close: plain Suave at the left edge, and indented blocks named page: , style: , props: and head: . counter.xsv props: start 0 count start def inc(): count + 1 page: div.counter: h2: Clicks: {count} button @click inc: Click me if count 5: p: That is a lot of clicking! style: .counter { padding: 1rem } A markup line is tag.class id attribute value ...: text . Leave out the tag and you get a div . Indented lines are its children. "quoted text" (or text ) is a plain text line. {name} puts a value in. if cond: , elif cond: , else: and for item in items: hold the lines under them. @click handler runs a function, @click "count + 1" runs a bit of code, bind:value {name} links a box to a variable, and class:done {cond} switches a class. Events: on:click {handler} or @click {handler} (a function; it gets the event if it has a parameter), or @click "count + 1" for a bit of code. The page redraws after every handler, and when you call update() . Two-way binding: bind:value {name} and bind:checked {item.done} . class:done {item.done} turns a class on and off. if "count 3" , else-if "..." , else , and for "item in items" or for "i, item in items" on any element. groups without adding an element. Child components: , with in the child for what is written between the tags. Names starting with a capital letter are components. A function called on mount() in the script runs after the first draw, and on unmount() when the component goes away. Styles are scoped to the component (they only touch its own elements). A .wsv page also takes a (title, meta, links) and mounts into app . suave new my-app --web a project with app.wsv and a counter component suave serve app.wsv build it and serve it at http://localhost:8000 suave build app.wsv -o dist dist/index.html (the page and every component it uses are inside) + dis

An app is three things: a state , a view that draws it, and an update that changes it. use std.dom fn view(state, dispatch) { dom.h("div", {}, [ dom.h("h1", {}, ["Count: {state}"]), dom.h("button", {on click: e dispatch("up")}, ["+1"]), ]) } fn update(state, msg) match msg { "up" state + 1, state } dom.app(" root", 0, view, update) dom.h(tag, props, children) makes a virtual node. Props: class , style (a map like {fontFamily: "serif"} ), value , checked , text , any attribute, and on click , on input , on change , on submit ... for events. An event is a map with value , checked , key , x , y , target and the functions prevent() and stop() . After every dispatch(msg) the page is patched, not rebuilt, so inputs keep focus. dom.query , dom.query all , dom.create , dom.on , dom.text , dom.attr , dom.add class , dom.value , dom.delegate , dom.download and more work on real elements if you prefer.

SUVL: Suave Values SUVL is Suave's own data format. It is meant for config files and data you edit by hand: friendly like YAML, exact like JSON, and typed like TOML. Files end in .suvl . a SUVL file name: "Ada Lovelace" tags: [math, poetry, 3.5] bare words are text; numbers, true, false, none are typed server { a block: key { ... } means key: { ... } host: localhost port: 8080 timeout: 90s durations become seconds cache: 64mb sizes become bytes ratio: 50% percentages become fractions (0.5) } born: 1815-12-10 dates and date-times become dates accent: ff8800 hex colors stay text point: {x: 1, y: 2} bio: """ Several lines, dedented to the least indented one. """

Entries. key: value (or key value ) or a block key { ... } . Entries end at a new line or a comma, so a: 1, b: 2 on one line is fine. A key is a bare word ( name , max-size , a.b ) or a quoted string. A key may appear only once in a map. Comments. and // run to the end of the line. A followed by 3, 4, 6 or 8 hex digits is a color, not a comment. Values. You write You get --- --- "text" with escapes \n \t \" \\ \u{1F600} text 'text' text, no escapes """...""" multi-line text, dedented hello /usr/bin a-b text (a bare word runs to a space, comma, bracket or quote) 42 -3.5 1e3 1 000 0xFF 0b101 0o17 numbers (huge whole numbers become big integers) inf -inf nan special numbers true false booleans none (or null ) none [a, b, c] list (commas or new lines between items; a trailing comma is fine) {a: 1, b: 2} map 2026-11-17 2026-11-17T10:30:00Z a date 90s 5m 2h 1d 1w 250ms seconds as a number ( 250ms is 0.25 ) 512b 4kb 10mb 1gb 2tb bytes as a number (1024 based) 50% a fraction ( 0.5 ) ff8800 text " ff8800" Use suvl.parse raw(text) to keep durations, sizes and percentages as text. The top level is normally a map. A whole file can also be a single list ( [1, 2, 3] ), a brace map, or a single value ( 42 ). An empty file is an empty map.

suvl.stringify(value) gives a canonical file: one entry per line, nested maps as blocks, short lists on one line, text bare when that is safe and quoted otherwise, dates as YYYY-MM-DD (or full date-times). Reading what you wrote gives the same value.

use std.suvl let cfg suvl.parse(fs.read("app.suvl")) print(cfg.server.timeout) // 90 fs.write("out.suvl", suvl.stringify({name: "x", tags: ["a", "b"]})) std.data can change a file between JSON, YAML, TOML, SUVL and CSV: suave convert app.yaml suvl .

Durations and sizes are first-class. timeout: 90s reads better than timeout seconds: 90 , and a wrong unit is a parse error. Bare words need no quotes , but everything is still unambiguous: only the listed words ( true , false , none , numbers, dates, units) change type, and the writer quotes any text that would be misread. Errors say where : line, column and the source line with a caret. It is small enough to hold in your head: one page.

Quantum computing and quantum mechanics in Suave Two modules and two language features work together: Complex and imaginary numbers are part of the language: 3 + 4i , 2.5i , abs(z) , sqrt(-4) . std.quantum is a quantum computer you can run: registers of qubits, gates, entanglement, measurement, circuit diagrams, and the famous algorithms. std.qm is quantum mechanics: hydrogen, particles in boxes, oscillators, tunneling, a Schrodinger equation solver, wave packets that move through time, spin and complex matrices. Pools (POOLS.md) are the language's own "undecided until observed" values.

let z 3 + 4i print(z z, z.conj(), abs(z), z.arg()) // -7 + 24i 3 - 4i 5 0.9273 print(sqrt(-4), 1i 2) // 2i -1 + 0i print(z.re, z.im) // 3 4 print(complex("1+2i"), complex(3, -1)) + - / work between complex numbers and ordinary numbers; compares both parts; complex numbers cannot be put in order ( < is an error: compare abs(z) ). Methods: re im abs arg conj norm sqrt exp ln pow sin cos tan sinh cosh tanh polar inv roots round is real . std.math functions ( sqrt exp ln sin cos pow abs ) accept them. std.complex adds roots of unity , quadratic , polyroots , fft , ifft , mandelbrot . Format specs apply to both parts: "{z:.2f}" .

use std.quantum as q let bell q.register(2) bell.h(0).cx(0, 1) // gates are chainable print(bell) // 0.7071 00 + 0.7071 11 print(bell.draw()) // a text circuit diagram print(bell.sample(1000)) // {"00": 497, "11": 503} Qubit order. Qubit 0 is the leftmost bit: 011 means qubit 0 is 0 and qubits 1 and 2 are 1. A register holds up to 22 qubits (the memory doubles with each one). Starting states: register(n) , basis("101") , plus(n) , bell(kind) , ghz(n) , w(n) , from amplitudes([1, 1i]) . Gates (each returns the register so you can chain): h x y z s t sdg tdg sx id (and h all , x all ...), rx ry rz p u (with angles), cx cy cz ch cp crx cry crz , ccx ccz mcx mcz , swap cswap , qft iqft , gate(matrix, qubit) for your own 2x2 unitary. phase oracle(f) flips the sign of every state where f(index) is true; permute(f) reorders states with a reversible function; diffusion() . Looking at a state: probs() (map), probabilities() (list), prob(q) , prob of("101") , amplitudes() , amplitude("01") , text() , bloch(q) , entanglement(q) (0 to 1 bit), is entangled() , expect("ZZ") , fidelity(other) , inner(other) , norm() , draw() , ops() , copy() , reset() . Measuring: measure(q) gives 0 or 1 and collapses the state; measure() measures every qubit (a list of bits); measure int() , measure text() . sample(shots) measures copies and leaves the register alone. measure later(q) gives a pool that measu

Call What it does --- --- q.grover(n, [11]) or q.grover(n, \ x\ x 11) search 2^n items in about sqrt of that many steps; gives found , probability , iterations , register q.deutsch jozsa(n, f) tells whether f is constant or balanced with ONE question q.bernstein vazirani("10110") finds a hidden bit string with one question q.teleport(a, b) sends the qubit a\ 0 + b\ 1 using entanglement and two classical bits; gives the fidelity q.shor(15) factors a number with quantum period finding (needs 3 qubits per bit of the number, so up to 127) q.random bits(8) , q.random int(10) , q.coin() true quantum randomness (as true as the simulator's generator) This is a simulator : it computes all the amplitudes on a normal computer, so it shows exactly what an ideal quantum computer would do, with no noise.

SI units unless a name ends in ev or nm . Wave functions are lists of numbers or complex numbers. use std.qm print(qm.hydrogen energy(1)) // -13.6057 (eV) print(qm.hydrogen transition(3, 2)) // the Balmer H-alpha line: 656.11 nm print(qm.box energy ev(1, 1e-9)) // 0.376 eV: an electron in a 1 nm box print(qm.tunneling(1, 2, 1, 1, 1)) // the chance of tunneling through a barrier // solve the Schrodinger equation for any potential (m hbar 1) let sol qm.solve 1d( x 0.5 x x, -8, 8, 500, k: 4) print(sol.energies) // [0.5, 1.4998, 2.4996, ...] // a wave packet moving through empty space let xs (0..256).map( i -20 + i 40 / 256) let psi qm.gaussian packet(xs, -5, 1, 2) // centre -5, width 1, momentum 2 let later qm.evolve(psi, 0, xs, dt: 0.05, steps: 100) print(qm.expect x(later, xs)) // about 5 Constants: h hbar c e m e m p m n eps0 mu0 k B N A a0 alpha R inf eV amu mu B G . Light and matter: photon energy ev photon wavelength nm photon frequency de broglie electron wavelength compton wavelength min momentum spread . Atoms: hydrogen energy hydrogen radius hydrogen transition hydrogen radial hydrogen density orbital name quantum numbers electron configuration rydberg wavelength nm . Simple systems: box energy box psi box probability oscillator energy oscillator psi tunneling hermite laguerre . Wave functions: solve 1d gaussian packet evolve norm probability expect x expect expect p spr

Pools: values that are decided when they are used A pool is a value that has not made up its mind yet. It holds several possible values (equally likely, or with weights), and it picks one the first time you use it . After that it stays decided. let weather pool ["rain", "sun", "snow"] print(inspect(weather)) // pool ["rain", "sun", "snow"] (undecided) let plans [weather, weather] // storing it does not decide it print("Today: {weather}") // using it does: now it is, say, "sun" print(weather, weather) // sun sun (it stays decided) Think of a coin in a closed hand, or a quantum state before you measure it.

pool [1, 2, 3] // equally likely pool 1.. 6 // a die pool {"heads": 9, "tails": 1} // weights: heads is nine times as likely pool random.rand() // a function: a fresh value every time it is decided pool(["a", "b"], weights: [3, 1]) // the function form pool [1, 2, 3].where( n n 1) // ask the pool itself: this is (pool [1, 2, 3]).where(...) pool takes just the next value, so pool [1, 2] + 1 means (pool [1, 2]) + 1 .

These decide it: arithmetic and comparison ( p + 1 , p < 3 ), if p , match p , printing it or putting it in a string, calling a method on it that is not a pool method ( p.upper() ), indexing ( p[0] ), looping over it, calling it, passing it to a built-in function ( print , len , str , sqrt ...), and p ?? x . These do not decide it: assigning it, putting it in a list or map, returning it, passing it to your own functions (the function decides when it uses it), and the pool methods below. A pool you share is the same pool everywhere, so when one place decides it, every place sees the same answer.

They never decide the pool. Method Gives --- --- is decided() true once it has been used peek() the decided value, or none if it is still open decide() decides it now and gives the value forget() makes it undecided again, so it can be decided afresh options() / size() the possible values / how many chances() a map from each value to its probability odds of(x) / most likely() the probability of x / the likeliest value where(f) a new pool that only keeps options for which f is true map(f) a new pool with f applied to every option with weights(list) a new pool with new weights roll() / rolls(n) fresh draws that leave the pool undecided simulate(n) how often each value comes up in n fresh draws entangle(other, ...) links pools (below) copy() an independent copy (undecided) inspect(p) shows a pool without deciding it. type(p) is "pool" , is pool(p) tests.

Pools that are entangled decide together: whichever is used first picks a position, and the others pick the same position. let shirt pool ["red", "green", "blue"] let shoes pool ["white", "black", "grey"] entangle(shirt, shoes) print("{shirt} with {shoes}") // red with white, green with black, or blue with grey They need the same number of options. forget() on one forgets them all.
Pools use the shared random generator, so random.seed(42) makes a whole program (pools, std.random and quantum measurements) give the same answers every run.

Ready-made pools: pool.die(6) , pool.dice("2d6+1") , pool.coin() , pool.weighted({...}) , pool.uniform(a, b) , pool.normal(mu, sigma) , pool.exponential(rate) , pool.poisson(l) , pool.shuffle(list) (a pool of orderings), pool.deal(list, k) (a hand of cards), pool.decide all(list) . Import it as use std.pool as pools if you also want to write pool [...] in the same file.

A quantum register can give you a pool that measures only when you look: reg.measure later(0) (the measurement really happens, and collapses the state, when the pool is first used) and reg.pool() (a weighted pool over all the possible outcomes that does not touch the register). See QUANTUM.md.

The Suave package manager suave has a package manager built in. A package is a folder with a suave.suvl file (in SUVL, Suave's data format). Installed packages go in suave modules/ and you use them with plain names: use mathx // the package's main file use mathx.extra as ex // mathx/extra.sv print(mathx.double(21)) Everything at the top of a package file whose name does not start with is public.

suave init [name] start a package (writes suave.suvl) suave add install and remember it (--dev for development-only ones) suave install install everything listed in suave.suvl suave install --frozen install exactly what suave.lock.suvl says, or fail suave update [name] get the newest versions that still fit suave remove uninstall (and anything only it needed) suave list what is installed suave pack make dist/ - .tar.gz suave publish --to add this package to a registry folder suave search look in the registry suave info versions of a package suave registry set where to look for packages

h: Where a package can come from
x: You write Meaning --- --- suave add mathx the newest version in your registry (recorded as mathx@^1.2.0 ) suave add mathx@^1.0 a version range: ^1.2.3 ~1.2 1.0.0 <2.0.0 1.x \ \ suave add path:../mathx a folder on this computer (copied in) suave add https://host/mathx-1.0.0.tar.gz a tarball on the web suave add github:user/repo or github:user/repo@v1.2 GitHub's source tarball for a branch, tag or commit

name: myapp version: 0.1.0 description: "What it does" entry: main.sv the file that "use myapp" and "suave run" start license: CC0-1.0 deps { mathx: "mathx@^1.2.0" helper: "path:../helper" } dev deps { } registry: "https://example.com/suave-registry" optional: where "suave add name" looks Names are lowercase letters, digits, - and , starting with a letter. Versions are 1.2.3 (semantic versions).

suave.lock.suvl records exactly what was installed: the version, where it came from, and a SHA-256 checksum of every download. suave install reuses it, and a download that does not match its checksum is refused : IntegrityError: The download for "mathx" 1.2.0 does not match its checksum ... I will not install it Keep the lock file with your project. Packages with a link inside them, or a file path that climbs out of the package ( ../ ), are never unpacked. A package is limited to 20 MB.

Installing a package also installs what it needs (its own deps ), into the same flat suave modules/ folder. If two packages ask for versions that cannot both be true, the first one wins and you get a warning that says who wanted what.

A registry is just a folder (or a web address) holding an index.suvl file and the packages. There is no central server to depend on: host the folder anywhere that serves static files. publish cd mathx suave publish --to ../my-registry packs it, adds it to my-registry/index.suvl use it (from a folder, or from a web address where you put that folder) suave registry set ../my-registry suave registry set https://example.com/suave-registry suave add mathx A published version can never be changed: publishing the same version again is an error, so bump version first. The index looks like this: name: "my registry" packages { mathx { description: "Extra maths helpers" versions { "1.2.0" { url: packages/mathx-1.2.0.tar.gz, sha256: "15faab..." } } } } The registry location is looked up in this order: registry in suave.suvl , the SUAVE REGISTRY environment variable, then ~/.suave/config.suvl (what suave registry set writes).
No official public registry yet (host your own, or use path: , tarball and github: sources), no package signing beyond the checksums, and no way to remove a published version.

Lake: tasks for your project A Lakefile (a plain Suave file named Lakefile ) lists the tasks of a project, like a Makefile, a Rakefile or the scripts of a Cargo project. Run them with lake (or suave lake ). Lakefile default task("build") task("build", desc "Build the website"): suave("build", "app.wsv", "-o", "dist") task("test", needs ["build"], desc "Run the tests"): suave("test") task("clean"): rm("dist") file("dist/site.zip", needs ["dist/index.html"]): sh("zip -r dist/site.zip dist") lake init make a starter Lakefile lake -l list the tasks, with their descriptions lake run the default task lake test run one task (what it needs runs first, each only once) lake build test several tasks lake -n all a dry run: show what would run lake mode fast -- one two vars (mode) and args (one, two) are available inside the Lakefile A task is a call with a colon block: task("name", needs [...], desc "...") followed by the indented lines. You can also write task("test", ["build"], "Run the tests") . file("path", needs [...]) is a task that is skipped when the file is newer than everything it needs. Lake looks for the Lakefile in the current folder and then the folders above it, and runs the tasks from the Lakefile's own folder. Things a Lakefile can call: sh("command") (add quiet true or check false ), suave("build", ...) (this same Suave), laker("build") , echo , rm , mkdir , cp , read , w

Laker: desktop apps for Suave Laker is to Suave what Tauri is to Rust: it turns a Suave web app (a .wsv page or your own index.html ) into a desktop app with its own window, and lets the page call a backend written in Suave. laker init "My App" laker.suvl, app.wsv, backend.sv laker dev build, serve and open the window laker build My App.app (a Mac app), or a folder with the program on Windows and Linux laker build --dmg on a Mac, also make a .dmg laker run open the built app laker.suvl holds the settings (name, id, version, entry, backend, icon, window size). backend.sv holds functions; every function whose name does not start with can be called from the page: backend.sv def greet(name): return "Hello, {name}!" app.wsv use std.laker async def ask(): greeting await laker.invoke("greet", {name: "Ada"}) std.laker also has info() , quit() , open url(url) , pick file() and pick save(name) (the operating system's file dialogs), read file(path) , write file(path, text) and is desktop() . The backend can use data dir() (a per-app folder), app dir() , os name() , plus all of Suave. How it works: the built app contains the Suave runtime (made with deno compile ) and your web files. When it opens it starts a small local server on a free port and shows the page in an app window, which is the Chrome, Edge, Brave or Chromium you already have, with no tabs or address bar (if none is installed
FAQ and troubleshooting {dual}

@item Is Radii Office really free? Yes. The apps are free to use, have no ads, and the code is open source. Anything you make is yours! @item Do I need an account? Not for the editing apps. You only need one for the server apps (Phosphor, Beta, Mintcode, Overshare and Yuzu mail), because they keep your data on a server! @item Where are my documents? In your browser's storage on this computer, or in a file if you chose Keep a file on this computer . Nothing is uploaded unless you share it! @item Can I use it offline? Yes. After the first visit the apps work without a connection. See Offline and desktop!

@item My tag stayed as plain text. Tags format when you press Space after them, or Enter at the end of the line. Check the symbols and the letters for a typo, then use Re-format , which underlines any tag that could not be formatted! @item I want to show a tag without using it. Put a backslash before its symbols, like \ R\ text\ , or put the tag in backticks! @item Which tag makes this look? Open the reference and use the filter. Every section has live examples!

@item A page is blank or old after an update. Do a hard refresh (Ctrl+Shift+R, or Cmd+Shift+R on a Mac). Apps are cached for offline use, and the new version loads on the next visit! @item My BitLang program ends instantly. Make sure you are in View mode, do not type in the page while it runs, and check the program for a stop() call. The error note shows how long it ran and why it ended! @item Real email in Yuzu shows as plain text. Only mail that arrived after the mail server's update has a formatted version, and you may have pressed Plain text on that message! @item Printing looks different from the screen.
